title: Protestants not abusing words: distinct names for distinct benefits
source_text: XXVI. Neque merito possunt accusari Protestantes, quod saltem hac in parte vocibus abutantur. Cum enim nostra a peccati poenis absolutio, & realis peccati in nobis deletio per infusionem novae justitiae, sint duo beneficia, connexa quidem & inseparabilia, sed natura tamen distincta; quidni Protestantibus licuerit, duo haec per naturam distincta, distinctis quoque vocibus, accuratioris doctrinae causa, in Scholis suis signare, ac priori gratiae nomen justificationis, posteriori vero sanctificationis nomen tribuere: Praesertim cum omnium consensu, justificandi vox in Scriptura sacra saepissime designet absolutionem judiciariam; & justificari dicatur, non qui reipsa justus efficitur, sed ille qui pro justo habetur atque reputatur.
pass_a_gloss: Nor can the Protestants deservedly be accused of abusing words, at least in this part. For since our absolution from the penalties of sin, and the real deletion of sin in us by the infusion of new righteousness, are two benefits, connected indeed and inseparable, yet distinct by nature; why should it not have been permitted to Protestants, for the sake of more accurate doctrine, to mark these two things distinct by nature with distinct words also in their Schools, and to assign to the former grace the name of justification, but to the latter the name of sanctification: especially since by the consent of all the word of justifying in sacred Scripture most often designates a judicial absolution; and he is said to be justified, not who is in very deed made just, but he who is held and reputed for just.
pass_b_english: Two inseparable but nature-distinct benefits deserve two school names: justification vs sanctification.
Scripture most often uses justify for judicial absolution / being reputed just.
